words: One that changed recently: US companies and US persons do not report beneficial ownership information to FinCEN; a final rule made this permanent from 14 August 2026.
The habit that keeps this clean in the books: one monthly expense report with receipts attached, reimbursed in a single payment. Do most founders you see run it monthly or quarterly?

Worth adding for e-filers: For tax year 2026, IRIS is the only IRS system for filing information returns electronically; the old FIRE system takes its last filings at 3 p.m. Eastern on Thursday 19 November 2026.
Clear way to put it. Which do you check first before an S corp election: steady profit, or whether the owner is ready to run payroll every month?
And for contractors paid $2,000 or more: Forms 1099-NEC for 2026 payments go to each payee and to the IRS by Monday 1 February 2027, since 31 January 2027 is a Sunday.
Agreed. What goes on your checklist for that review: cash on hand, what's set aside for taxes, or unpaid invoices?
Interesting gap. When owners bring a decision to the table this time of year, is it more often about hiring, pricing, or how much cash to keep in reserve?
Good question to ask. Of the owners you work with, how many found out about the default classification only when the first return was due?
The one-lump-sum trap is so common. Do you move the Profit First percentages every time a payment lands, or on a set schedule? Curious which rhythm stuck for you.
Clear line between an employee and a co-founder. What's your test for a technical co-founder before the equal split: a small project built together first, or conversations alone?
Good tip for small shops. How do you keep an eye on the other states during the year: a quick monthly look at sales by state, or one check at year end?
One change for that year-end list: For payments made in 2026, Form 1099-NEC reports nonemployee compensation of $2,000 or more paid to a payee; the threshold was $600 before.
That receipt hour adds up fast. Do you attach each receipt to its transaction the day you pay, or batch them all at month end?
One from the finance side: know your runway in months, not just your bank balance, and update it every month. Founders who see the date coming raise on their terms instead of in a rush.

Whichever bank wins, open the account in the company's name from day one and run every business dollar through it. Clean separation makes the books, the tax return and any investor's diligence far simpler.
Good one to flag. The habit that helps most early on: set aside part of each payment in its own savings account as it comes in, so the tax money is already there when it's due.

Good reminder. Payment apps and other third party settlement organizations are not required to file Form 1099-K for a payee unless the year's payments to that payee exceed $20,000 and the transactions exceed 200. So your own records matter.

Bookkeeping making the list makes sense. The step worth keeping human is the monthly match of the books' cash balance to the bank statement, where a missed or duplicated transaction shows up. Did the survey break that out?
One to add to the W-9 step: ask a foreign contractor for Form W-8BEN, or Form W-8BEN-E from a foreign company; a valid W-8 exempts the payment from Form 1099 reporting and backup withholding.
Congrats! One thing you can cross off: US companies and US persons do not report beneficial ownership information to FinCEN; a final rule made this permanent from 14 August 2026.
Fair point for a lot of side hustles. Where do you usually draw the line: once there's real liability, like employees or a lease, or once outside investors are in the picture?
Great example. For consumer brands, do the customers who already buy the product usually make up most of the investors, or does the platform bring in mostly new faces?
Every quarter it stings! The habit that helps: move a set share of each payment into its own tax savings account the day it lands, so the bill is already waiting when it's due.
And for contractors outside the US: ask a foreign contractor for Form W-8BEN, or Form W-8BEN-E from a foreign company; a valid W-8 exempts the payment from Form 1099 reporting and backup withholding.

Exactly, and apps are a big reason. Payment apps and other third party settlement organizations are not required to file Form 1099-K for a payee unless the year's payments to that payee exceed $20,000 and the transactions exceed 200.

For a lot of owners it's the books: a month of uncategorized transactions piling up. A short weekly habit of matching receipts as they come in, then one bank reconciliation at month end, keeps it small.
Agreed. When that founder with an audience does raise, what do you see them trip on first: the numbers behind the traction, or paperwork like a cap table nobody kept up?
Well put. A named competitor also gives your numbers a yardstick: their pricing and growth make your own projections easier for an investor to believe, or to question.
One date that answers the January question for many owners: Forms 1099-NEC for 2026 payments go to each payee and to the IRS by Monday 1 February 2027, since 31 January 2027 is a Sunday.
Clear graphic, and the bottom line is the key part. When a client has many small payers, what record do you ask them to keep through the year: a simple log by payer, or the bank deposits?
Agreed. The weekly check that pays off most: compare the books' bank balance with the real one. A gap usually means something is missing or doubled, and a week's worth is quick to find.
Great line on partners. On the cap table side, what's the first item on your diligence list: how they behaved in a past down round, or what rights they ask for in the paperwork?

Worth adding to the S corp math: the reasonable salary runs through payroll, with its own filings and fees, so the savings are what's left after those costs. Clean monthly books make that comparison quick.
Number 3 is easy to check. On Y Combinator's post-money SAFE, the ownership sold is known at signing: $1 million at a post-money valuation cap of about $6.7 million is about 15% of the company.
So true, knowing and doing are different jobs. Which part trips up your S corp clients more once payroll is live: settling on the salary number, or keeping the pay runs regular all year?
Great timing for it. While going through the list, note which card each subscription bills to, so nothing renews unnoticed and the year-end books match the statements.
Unbilled work is a big one: the extra hour or quick favor for a client that never makes it onto an invoice. Comparing what was delivered with what was billed each month turns it up.
Another for startups with developers abroad: research and experimental costs for work done outside the US must still be spread over 15 years.
One January date to plan around: Forms 1099-NEC for 2026 payments go to each payee and to the IRS by Monday, February 1, 2027, since January 31, 2027 is a Sunday.
Interesting jump. Did the survey split out what owners mean by taxes: the size of the bill, or the paperwork and deadlines around it? Those two call for very different fixes.
More revenue without a budget usually means spending rises to match it. Even a simple monthly check of actual spending against plan shows where the extra money went before it's gone.
Bookkeeping tends to top that list because it compounds: a week of receipts is a twenty minute job, a quarter of them is a project. Putting it on the calendar like a client meeting helps.
